PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:12:A mobile-first web platform that connects natural-method farmers in Andhra Pradesh directly with local buyers, with optional home delivery by local delivery riders.
PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:20:The platform works entirely in a web browser. There is **nothing to download** — a buyer simply opens a link, browses produce from farmers around them, adds items to a cart, and places an order. Farmers get their own profile pages and a simple dashboard to list produce, manage prices, accept or decline orders, and confirm payments. Local delivery riders can sign up, get approved by the owner, and deliver orders to the buyer's door.
PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:24:The system currently supports the full cycle: a farmer lists produce → a buyer orders and pays via UPI (or Cash on Delivery where the farmer allows it) → the farmer confirms → the order is either picked up or delivered to the buyer's home by a rider.
PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:44:| No delivery option | Buyers must travel to the farm to collect produce |
PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:56:- Allows buyers to **order online and pay via UPI**, with the farmer confirming payment manually, or pay **Cash on Delivery** where the farmer allows it.
PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:57:- Offers **home delivery** through local riders who are vetted and approved by the platform owner.
PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:68:5. Provide an optional, reliable home-delivery service via local riders.
PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:83:| **Delivery Rider** | Local delivery agents | Sign up, accept delivery jobs, pick up and deliver orders |
PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:84:| **Owner / Admin** | The platform operator | Approve riders, oversee deliveries, reassign orders |
PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:94:                   │   Buyer / Farmer / Rider /   │
PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:114:        │  produce, riders…)│              │  payment proofs,    │

PROJECT_DOCUMENTATION.md:121:- **One app, four "doorways."** Buyers, farmers, riders, and the owner each get their own login and their own screens, but it is all one website.

**Step 3 — The order waits for the farmer.**
The order sits there marked "delivery, nobody assigned yet." Riders cannot see it. Nothing happens until the farmer confirms the order.

**Step 4 — The farmer confirms. Now riders can see it.**
The moment the farmer confirms, the order appears in the job list of every active rider whose service area matches the buyer's pincode. The farmer's "Mark Shipped" button is also switched off for this order, because a rider is going to handle the handoff, not the farmer.

**Step 5 — A rider takes the job.**
Two ways this happens, and both already exist:
- The **rider grabs it** themselves from their list of available jobs, or
- The **owner assigns it** to a specific rider from the admin panel.

Before accepting, the rider only sees the produce, the pincode, and the payout. They do **not** see the buyer's name, phone, or street until they've actually accepted the job.

**Step 6 — The rider delivers it.**
Four taps, in order: *Accepted* → *Picked up from farm* → *Out for delivery* → *Delivered*. To finish, the rider must type in the buyer's 4-digit handover code at the door. No correct code, no completed delivery. That's the proof the right person got the food.

**Step 7 — Before any of this, the rider had to be approved.**
A rider signs up at `/rider/signup`, uploads their ID, and declares which pincodes they cover. They then sit as "pending" until the **owner approves them** in the admin panel. Only approved, active riders ever see a single job. The owner can also suspend or reinstate them later.

The database was designed to default to `'pending_approval'` — the migration says so explicitly, and the intended lifecycle is written right there in the comment: *pending_approval → approved (with activation code) → active*. Now I understand the whole picture. **There are two completely separate rider systems in this codebase, and they don't talk to each other.**

## The two systems

**`delivery_boys`** — the real one. Riders self-sign up at `/rider/signup`, log in, see jobs, accept them, and deliver. Every rider route, the admin panel, order assignment, and the handover code all run on this table. **This is what actually delivers food.** And as I found earlier, signup auto-activates — no vetting.

**`delivery_agents`** — the moderator's "Delivery agents" page. The moderator types in a name, phone, Aadhaar (stored as a one-way hash), vehicle, area, and availability. It's zone-scoped and looks exactly like the vetting screen you're describing.

**But it's a phonebook.** Nothing is wired to it. Only two files in the entire codebase touch `delivery_agents` — the two moderator routes that read and write it. An agent in that table has **no login, no password, and no connection to any order.** They can never see or deliver anything. The migration comment even admits it: *"a standalone roster, separate from the rider self-signup `delivery_boys`."*

So right now the moderator carefully vets people who can't deliver, while anyone who fills in the public signup form instantly can.

## What we have to build

The fix is to **make the moderator's screen govern the real table** — one system instead of two:

1. **Registration stops auto-activating.** `/rider/signup` inserts `status: 'pending_approval'` instead of `'active'`. The rider gets a "we'll review and call you" screen.
2. **Pending riders can't get in.** Login currently only blocks `suspended`; it must also hold back anyone not yet active.
3. **The moderator's "Delivery agents" page reads `delivery_boys`.** It shows pending applications with everything the rider submitted — name, phone, alt phone, vehicle type and number, service areas, pincodes — plus **a viewable link to their uploaded ID photo** (it's in a private bucket, so this needs a short-lived signed URL). Then: **Approve**, **Reject**, and later **Suspend / Reinstate**.
4. The approve/suspend/reinstate logic already exists and is correct in `/api/admin/riders/*` — it just needs to be callable by a moderator, not only the owner.

That's genuinely most of a day's work, not a rewrite. The delivery machinery underneath is fine.

**Second — zone scoping.** Moderators are scoped to a zone (`tadepalligudem` etc.), but `delivery_boys` has no zone column — riders only declare **pincodes**. So either a moderator sees every pending rider platform-wide, or we add a zone to riders and map it. Yes, region matching exists — but it's **exact pincode matching**, and it's only skin-deep. Here's the honest picture.

## How the matching actually works

A rider declares one or more **6-digit pincodes** at signup ("I cover 530026"). When their job list loads, the system shows only orders whose delivery pincode is an **exact string match** to one of theirs.

That's it. It's not a radius, not a distance, not "nearby." There's no map, no GPS, no district or region logic. **530026 and 530027 could be two streets apart and the rider would never see the second one.** Pincode matching is all-or-nothing.

This is exactly why your 17 orders are stranded. `vijay` declared 530026 (Visakhapatnam). The orders are in 534102 — a different district entirely. Not a near-miss; genuinely nobody covers that area.

## Two holes in it, though

**The pincode filter is cosmetic.** It only decides what a rider *sees* on their screen. When a rider actually taps Accept, the server checks that the order is home-delivery, approved, and unclaimed — **it never re-checks the pincode.** So any active rider who knows an order's ID can accept *any* delivery in the country, in an area they never signed up for, and immediately get the buyer's name, phone, and home address.

Stack that on top of the auto-activation I found earlier and the full path is: a stranger fills in the public signup form → is instantly active → accepts any order anywhere → gets a customer's home address. That's the thing to close.

**A rider with zero pincodes sees everything.** If `service_pincodes` is empty, the filter is skipped entirely and the rider sees every unassigned delivery on the platform. Signup now requires at least one pincode, so this only affects older accounts — but the escape hatch is still in the code.

content.text:
Built, migrated, and verified against the real database. Nothing is committed or pushed — that's yours to call.

## What now happens

A rider signs up at `/rider/signup` as before, but the application lands as **pending** instead of going live. They see "we'll review it and call you," and they cannot log in. The moderator opens **Delivery riders** in the sidebar, sees the application in a "Waiting" tab with the name, phone, vehicle, declared areas, and **the ID photo itself** rendered inline (via a 10-minute signed URL — the bucket stays private). They type the pincodes that rider is actually allowed to cover, and hit Approve. Only then can the rider log in and see jobs.

Approving requires at least one pincode, so nobody gets approved into an empty job list. The moderator's pincode grant overrides whatever the rider claimed at signup — self-declared areas are a request, not a grant. Suspended and rejected riders are locked out immediately.

## The security hole I found and closed

This is the part worth knowing about. **The pincode filter was decorative.** It controlled what a rider *saw*, but the accept endpoint never re-checked it — so any active rider could POST any order ID and claim a delivery anywhere in the country, which immediately hands them the buyer's **name, phone, and home address**. Stacked on the auto-activation, the full path was: stranger fills in the public form → instantly live → grabs any order → gets a customer's address.

I verified the fix by actually running the attack. Signed in as `vijay` (covers 530026 only), I tried to accept one of the stranded 534102 orders:

```
HTTP 403  {"error":"This delivery is outside your service area."}
```

and confirmed in the database that the order row was **not** touched — still unassigned, no rider, no timestamp. His own job feed correctly shows his 16 orders in 530026 and nothing else. I also removed the "rider with no pincodes sees every order on the platform" fallback.

One correction to something I told you earlier: I said suspending a rider leaves their in-flight deliveries accessible. That's wrong — `/api/rider/me` requires `active`, so a suspended rider is cut off instantly and anything they were already carrying must be reassigned from the owner panel. The code comment says so now.

## Two things I want to flag

**The migration is already applied to production.** I ran it against your live Supabase, so the columns exist now — but the *code* isn't deployed. That's the safe order (columns are additive and unused until the code ships), and `scripts/rider-approval-migration.sql` is checked in for the record. Your existing rider `vijay` is untouched and still active.

**Your git repo has a corrupt object** — `git log` dies on `loose object c28136071… is corrupt`. It's unrelated to this work but it will bite you on the next push. Worth fixing before you commit.

Want me to commit this, and should I also add that owner-panel alert for delivery orders sitting in pincodes no rider covers? That's still the reason 17 orders are stranded — this change doesn't fix that on its own, it just means you can now approve a rider for 534102 and have them actually get the jobs.
